newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Analysts hail Argentina's quick financing strategy.
newsitem.headline: Analysts hail Argentina's quick financing strategy.

text.p: Argentina kicked off 1997 with the announcement of its biggest debt deal since its Brady plan in 1993 and analysts said it all bodes well for the country's ambitious financing plans for the first half of the year.

After weeks of speculation, Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said Tuesday Argentina will launch a two-tranche, $2.0 billion global bond consisting of a five- and a 20-year fixed rate bullet issue. The issues will be placed in the second half of this month.

Analysts said the Economy Ministry's strategy in the run-up to, and the actual confirmation of the bond, is a sign of Fernandez's predictable style, something that bodes well for the placement of the issue.
"This team's strategy is obviously to come with no surprises -- it's a smart, very prudent strategy," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings.
Fernandez started hinting at a big global issue in December.
The one surprise element of the announcement was the planned launch of another $1.0 billion bond issue before the end of March.

As an assurance to investors whose biggest worry about investing in Argentina this year is the October mid-term Congressional elections, Fernandez said most of the budgeted borrowing this year will have been financed when the $2 billion issue is placed.

With the total $3.0 billion of these issues and the $2.0 billion worth of bonds already sold in December covering 1997 spending needs, only $3.5 billion of the $8.5 billion in new debt slated for this year remains to be placed.
"It is good not having that (financing) cloud in investors minds" when the elections take place, added Thomsen.
Apart from that, the perception that U.S. rates will rise through the year makes it a smart move to issue a lot of debt early in the year.

"They (the government) are thinking U.S. Treasury yields will rise gradually through the year, so they are issuing early to secure lower rates of borrowing," said Marina Kessler, a bond analyst at Banco Frances del Rio de la Plata.
Analysts welcomed the decision by the ministry to issue another $1.0 billion bond by the end of March rather than one large $3.0 billion.
"I think that went well with some of the foreign investors," said an analyst at a foreign bank in Buenos Aires.

In addition, "I am sure they have offers" to underwrite the $1.0 billion issue, added the analyst. "I know of another two or three banks that offered for the big one -- they will be interested in the other issue."
Merrill Lynch & Co and J.P. Morgan will be lead managers of the $2.0 billion issue.

Although there is some concern by investors that these Argentine bonds combined with a Mexican 10-year fixed rate issue expected to be priced this week will lead to an oversupply in the Eurobond market, the fact that Merrill is involved in the Argentine issue is positive news, added the foreign bank analyst.

"When a new bank gets into an issue, it's pretty good news," he said, referring to the fact that Merrill has not underwritten a big issue of this kind for some time, meaning it may have a larger pool of its own clients waiting to pick up the paper.

Also, say market players, the fact that it is a straight fixed-coupon bullet issue may help generate interest by investors who are not accustomed to Argentina's other foreign bonds, most of which amortize over the life of the bond and pay floating interest. A bullet issue has no early redemption facility.
